nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: How can implementing the GUTB method affect tractor efficiency?
nodes.answer: Implementing the GUTB method can lead to significant improvements in fuel and tractive efficiency for both two- and four-wheel drive tractors.
nodes.paragraph: On-farm energy use and energy useef ciency in small-holder agriculture settings were con- sidered to be outside the scope of this work and as such they merit a separate analysis. Hence, it is recommendedthat this work is expanded by undertaking a similar review analysis relevant to small landholder farming systems. Techniques for Optimizing Tractor Fuel Consumption Adaptive Driving: Gear-up and Throttle-back Gear-up and throttle-back (GUTB) is a fuel-saving practice that has been popular around the world since the fuel crisis of the mid-1970s. The GUTB technique can be imple-mented to save fuel when drawbar loads are light ( \75% of rated power) and power take-off (PTO) speed can be reduced [ 34]. This method improves engine ef ciency by maintaining high engine load and an engine speed at 60 80% of rated speed [ 35]. Signi cant improvements in fuel and tractive ef ciency from implementation of thismethod were achieved with two- and four-wheel drive tractors in Canada [ 69]. For maximum operating ef ciency, a tractor engine should be operated near its rated capacity.Many eld operations such as light tillage, planting, mechanical weed control, spraying, and hay-raking, how- ever, do not require full tractor power.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_001
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: Why will economic incentives only permit the achievement of 10%-15% of the emission reduction potential?
nodes.answer: Economic incentives will only permit the achievement of 10%-15% of the emission reduction potential due to the high costs associated with implementing mitigation practices like feed supplementation or manure treatment.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_002
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What are the impacts of manure application methods on emissions of ammonia, nitrous oxide, and crop response according to J. Webb, B. Pain, S. Pittman, J. Morgan's review?
nodes.answer: According to the review by J. Webb, B. Pain, S. Pittman, J. Morgan, different manure application methods can have varying impacts on emissions of ammonia, nitrous oxide, and crop response. Some methods may result in higher emissions of these gases while others may lead to better crop responses.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_003
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What are some technical options for mitigating direct methane and nitrous oxide emissions from livestock, as discussed in the review by Gerber et al. (2013)?
nodes.answer: Some technical options for mitigating direct methane and nitrous oxide emissions from livestock include dietary interventions, manure management strategies, and genetic selection for low-emission livestock breeds, as outlined in the review by Gerber et al. (2013).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_004
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How can effective laws and appropriate technologies help mitigate GHG emissions resulting from the increasing meat consumption in Argentina?
nodes.answer: By implementing effective laws and utilizing appropriate technologies, it is possible to mitigate GHG emissions resulting from the increasing meat consumption in Argentina.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_005
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How can taxonomic categorization of bovine breeds help mitigate GHG emissions in animal commodities?
nodes.answer: Taxonomic categorization of bovine breeds can assist in identifying breeds that are more environmentally friendly, thus contributing to the reduction of GHG emissions per unit of animal commodities.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_006
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Why is it crucial for the animal product supply chain to promote the utilization of low-carbon energy resources?
nodes.answer: Promoting the use of low-carbon energy resources in the animal product supply chain is vital because fossil fuels are a significant contributor to GHG emissions in cattle production, making it imperative to lower carbon footprints for sustainability.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_007
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How can decarbonize electricity generation reduce GHG emissions from cattle systems?
nodes.answer: Decarbonized electricity generation has the potential to reduce GHG emissions originating from cattle systems. According to Lynch and Pierrehumbert (2019), implementing decarbonized electricity can help lower emissions in the agricultural sector.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_008
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How can acidification of liquid manure help enhance management practices and mitigate losses associated with manure storage?
nodes.answer: Acidification of liquid manure can be an effective strategy for enhancing management practices and mitigating losses associated with manure storage, as stated by We et al. (2023).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_009
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What is an economically viable method to reduce emissions related to manure management?
nodes.answer: According to Liu and Liu (2018), implementing manure energy recovery can help reduce emissions if it is economically viable.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_010
nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What are some potential mitigation strategies for reducing GHG emissions in the livestock sector of Argentina?
nodes.answer: Potential mitigation strategies include transitioning from beef to chicken or plant-based protein alternatives, adopting high-efficiency farming practices, using low-carbon energy sources, and expanding circular agriculture.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_011
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How can the greenhouse gas emissions of self-selected individual diets in France be reduced according to Lieux et al. (2012)?
nodes.answer: According to Lieux et al. (2012), greenhouse gas emissions of self-selected individual diets in France can be reduced by either changing the diet structure or consuming less.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_013
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: Have there been studies in the UK investigating multiple mitigation measures for beef production systems using LCA?
nodes.answer: No, there have not been studies investigating multiple mitigation measures via a data-driven scenario analysis in this area.
nodes.paragraph: The authors highlighted that medium duration (i.e. 18 24 months) grassland-based beef production systems in Scotland were found to achieve a balance between financial returns and environmental performance. A study comprising sites in different nations in the UK (Cardenas et al. 2019) found that NUE depended on the type of N fertiliser, and although NUE increased with fertiliser rate, so did the emis- sions of N2O. Measures such as application of inhibitors and splitting N application were effective in improving NUE in these grasslands. More recently, using qualitative methods, different mitigation measures in the UK agricultural sector were synthesised based on the existing scientific literature and elicitation of expert opinions (Buckingham et al. 2023; Jebari et al. 2023). Nevertheless, due to system interac- tions, mitigation practices that reduce emissions in one stage may increase emissions elsewhere, and mitigation practices must therefore be evaluated at the whole farm level (Montes et al. 2013 ). To the best of our knowl - edge, there have not been studies in the UK investigating multiple mitigation measures via a data-driven scenario analysis with respect to grassland, grazing, and manure management of beef production systems using LCA.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Greenhouse gas emission reduction|Livestock methane reduction_qna_014
nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What measures are suggested to encourage sustainable practices in livestock production?
nodes.answer: The review suggests that measures need to be implemented to encourage sustainable practices while minimizing trade-offs, though specific measures are not detailed in the provided text.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract How do agricultural policies in the EU need to change to increase the sustainability of livestock production, and what meas- ures could encourage sustainable practices whilst minimising trade-offs? Addressing such questions is crucial to ensure progress towards proclaimed targets whilst moving production levels to planetary boundaries. However, a lack of available evidence on the impacts of recent policies hinders developments in this direction. In this review, we address this knowledge gap, by collating and evaluating recent policy analyses, using three complementary frameworks. The review highlights that recent policy reforms, and especially those of the Common Agricultural Policy, have had a large impact on the sustainability of the livestock sector by contributing to intensification and simplification. This has often resulted in negative impacts (e.g. on greenhouse gas emissions and animal welfare) and while financial support has enabled production, it can also lead to a culture of dependency that limits innovation. At the same time, a lack of regulation and concrete targets, and low levels of stakeholder engagement in policy design have led to delays in the delivery of sustainability objectives.
